Text | Er Mu

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

First, take a look at this fun video:

Watch the video: one man, two voices! The beats and the chords, at the same time!

Having watched it, can you tell whether the man in the video is doing the backing track or the vocals?

The answer is that he is doing both. That sounds a bit unbelievable. Common sense tells us that a person can only make one sound at a time.

The video above is “If Your Mother Only Knew,” a widely shared, legendary performance by the famous American beatboxer Rahzel. Before he launches into it, he tells the audience he is going to do five things at once: “[I’m] going to do the beat, right, the chorus, the bass line, the verse, and the background vocals.”

Here is a more complete video:

So how does Rahzel do it?

In beatboxing, the backing beat is produced at the front of the mouth, and the sung vocals by the vocal folds in the larynx. Really skilled performers such as Rahzel can indeed make both parts sound at the same time. Even so, the limits of the human vocal apparatus mean the two sounds cannot come out fully independent and distinct: what actually emerges is a blend of the two. So why do we end up hearing two separate, clear sounds produced simultaneously?

That’s right, you guessed it: the answer lies in us. Rahzel is playing a little trick, exploiting the way our brain processes “fragments” of sound.

The video below demonstrates one such mechanism: illusory continuity.

In the video you hear an intermittent beep, with a short burst of noise between each pair of beeps. As the burst gets louder, the beeps gradually seem to join up into one continuous pure tone (tip: it works even better with your eyes closed). But this is only an illusion created by our brain. The beep never changes from start to finish: it is always intermittent. Our brain invents a continuous tone even though it isn’t there.

In the video, the frequency of the beep is constant. In fact, whether the frequency is constant, falling or rising, as long as the noise bursts are loud enough we hear a continuous tone. Listen to the recording below: a continuously rising pure tone is interrupted by bursts of narrowband noise. The noise is fairly loud, yet the tone still sounds as if it rises continuously, with no sense of interruption.

Beatboxers can genuinely exploit this gap between the sound our brain perceives and the sound that actually enters our ears. Rahzel can produce two sounds at once, but the drum beat is sometimes not quite right. We can’t hear the difference because our brain can’t tell the faulty beat from a normal one and assumes nothing has changed.

Another trick Rahzel uses: before the performance proper, he spends a long time singing the lyrics and melody on their own, so the audience gets to know them in advance. When he then adds a not-quite-normal drum beat, the audience is much less likely to notice. Primed by what they’ve already heard, listeners automatically fill in the correct beat themselves.

Doesn’t what Rahzel does seem a bit like a magician who uses a glamorous assistant to distract the audience while he quietly pulls off his sleight of hand?

Filling in fragments of sound so that they become continuous, connected passages is a really important skill. It is what lets us follow what someone is saying in a noisy environment.

It reminded me of two famous passages of text:

In both passages above, one Chinese and one English, the characters or letters are scrambled, yet that hardly gets in the way of reading. That, too, is the brain filling in the gaps.

So filling in the gaps really matters!!!

How good is your brain at it?
